item.title: The Psychology of Minimalism
item.description:
Environment

The Psychology of Minimalism

The mental benefits of having only what you need.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Minimalism helps people feel more in control of their lives and clearer headed.
  • Minimalism also saves time. The less possessions you have, the less time spent organizing them.
  • If you want to be more minimalist, make decluttering and donating belongings a regular habit.
Source: Photo by Inside Weather on Unsplash

Now that I have a five and a nine-year-old, I feel like my role has shifted to Organizer of All the Things. My children have acquired a quantity of toys and clothes that feels overwhelming and relentless.

When it was just me, I lived in a studio apartment. It was about 300 square feet of minimalist simplicity. I had the exact right amount of clothes and books. I could imagine in my mind’s eye all my possessions because everything had its place. Even though it was a tiny apartment, there was room to breathe because of the lack of clutter.

Now, I’m constantly battling other people’s possessions. They’re kids, so they tend toward maximalism. More is more is more. Sometimes it seems that none of us even know where these belongings came from. They seem to reproduce on their own accord, and no organizational system seems to keep them tidy.

Inevitably, they pile up in a way that makes me snap. I tear through their rooms with big black garbage bags, asking the girls which things we can donate. They comply because they know more stuff is on the way. There are birthdays and holidays. There are aunts and grandmas soon to visit, bearing gifts, of course.

The Psychological Benefits of Minimalism

Minimalism has its mental benefits. In one interview-based study, participants reported that they’d arrived at their minimalist lifestyles due to autonomy or competence. The burden that clutter brought prompted many people to choose another path, one where they could better align their lives, free from overwhelming amounts of possessions. Less belongings also helped some people feel more competent, like they had more control over their lives.

Owning too many things means managing too many things. The more belongings one has, the more time must be spent organizing and thinking about those things.

I’m not the only one who feels better when all their things have a place. Participants of the study also reported feeling clear-headed when inhabiting a minimalist environment.

Source: Photo by Bench Accounting on Unsplash

How to Be More Minimalist

To feel freer, more competent, and mentally free, there are a few things you can try. My favorite minimalist move is to constantly be decluttering. Instead of trying to figure out where everything should go, I always declutter as I clean. It’s easier to get rid of something than create a new organizational system for it to fit in your home.

Use every cleaning opportunity as a chance to rid your life of unnecessary possessions.

Another trick is to have as many blank surfaces as you can. Stop filling every shelf, and see how you feel when there’s more room to breathe.

Finally, remove some of your storage. The more shelves and drawers and bins you have, the more you’ll fill them with stuff. Don’t fall into the trap of thinking that your organizational system is going to save you from your clutter. Less storage means fewer belongings.

None of this gets at the root cause of why we over-consume in the first place, but thinking about how good you’ll feel when your space is more minimalist might be just the thing you need to simplify your life.

In the meantime, I’ll be roaming my house like a maniac, searching for excess, desperately trying to cut through the clutter and live more simply and freely.

item.title: Why Intelligent People Fall for Bad Arguments
item.description:
Persuasion

Why Intelligent People Fall for Bad Arguments

What the Sophists, Plato, and Aristotle can teach us about persuasion and truth.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Intelligence alone cannot protect us from bad arguments.
  • The Sophists, Plato, and Aristotle transformed the study of persuasion and truth.
  • We embrace bad arguments because they satisfy psychological needs, not logical ones.
The Sophists taught people how to win arguments. Plato and Aristotle asked whether they were also true.
Source: Neel Burton

History is full of brilliant people who believed ridiculous things. Isaac Newton devoted years to searching for the philosopher’s stone. Thomas Edison promoted radioactive products as health remedies. Steve Jobs believed that his vegan diet made regular bathing unnecessary.

The problem isn’t that intelligent people cannot think. It’s that they’re human.

We like to imagine that reason is an impartial judge, carefully weighing evidence before arriving at a verdict. More often, it behaves like a defence lawyer, marshalling arguments for conclusions we reached for entirely different reasons.

Our hopes, fears, loyalties, ambitions, and prejudices all shape the way we reason. We are naturally drawn to arguments that flatter our opinions, excuse our behaviour, or confirm our suspicions. And the more intelligent we are, the more ingenious our rationalizations can become.

The ancient Greeks understood this all too well.

Persuasion Versus Truth

In democratic Athens, success increasingly depended on persuasion. Citizens defended themselves in the law courts, debated policy in the Assembly, and competed for influence with words rather than swords. A new class of professional teachers, known as the Sophists, arose to teach this art of argument.

Their lessons were practical rather than philosophical. They taught their students—often young, wealthy aristocrats—how to sway an audience, defend either side of a case, and even make the weaker argument appear the stronger.

For Plato, this represented a profound problem. His beloved teacher, Socrates, had been condemned to death by a jury persuaded more by rhetoric than by reason. If eloquence—or simple pandering—could triumph over truth, what hope was there for philosophy?

Plato’s pupil Aristotle responded by laying the foundations of logic and identifying the many ways in which arguments can go wrong. If rhetoric explains how people are persuaded, logic lays out when they ought to be.

Yet beneath this history lies an uncomfortable lesson.

Bad arguments rarely persuade us because they are logically compelling. They persuade us because they satisfy some psychological need.

article continues after advertisement

An ad hominem attack invites us to judge the speaker rather than the argument. A straw man offers an easier opponent to defeat. An appeal to popularity reassures us that millions of other people cannot be wrong. A false dilemma offers clarity where reality is usually more complicated. Circular reasoning allows us to begin with the conclusion we wanted all along.

Each exploits a different human weakness. Together, they encourage us to condemn our opponents, sidestep the real issue, follow the crowd, crave certainty, and believe what we wanted to believe all along.

Why We Fall for Bad Arguments

Plato feared that rhetoric had become detached from truth, while Aristotle sought to distinguish valid reasoning from mere persuasion. But neither believed that bad arguments prevailed simply because people lacked intelligence. They prevailed because they appealed to pride, fear, tribal loyalties, wishful thinking, and our deep desire to be right.

That is why exposing a fallacy so seldom changes anyone’s mind. We do not cling to bad arguments because we are in need of illumination. We cling to them because they satisfy needs that logic alone serves to undermine.

The Sophists discovered that winning an argument is not the same as finding the truth. Plato and Aristotle devoted much of their philosophy to closing the gap between the two. More than two thousand years later, that remains one of our most important tasks—and one at which we keep on backsliding.

History is still full of brilliant people who believe ridiculous things—not because they cannot think, but because they are human.

A version of this post also appears on the author's website.

item.title: When Criticism Turns Into Justification
item.description:
Schadenfreude

When Criticism Turns Into Justification

Why we start defending harm once we think the target deserves it.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • We often shift from judging actions to judging whether the target “deserves” them.
  • When a target feels deserving, harmful responses start to feel more acceptable.
  • What looks like hypocrisy often reflects which values are active in the moment.
Source: Image AI-generated with ChatGPT 5.3 / OpenAI

It doesn’t always stop at criticism.

Someone says something online—offensive, careless, sometimes just poorly worded—and the response escalates quickly. At first, it looks like what you’d expect: disagreement, pushback, maybe some ridicule. But in some cases, it becomes quite extreme.

People start trying to figure out who the person is. Where they work. How to contact them. Personal details get surfaced and shared. What began as criticism starts to look more like targeting.

And when it crosses that line, the reaction often isn’t This went too far. It’s something closer to: Well… they kind of had it coming.

That shift is easy to miss, but it matters because once that reaction takes hold, people aren’t really asking whether the response itself is acceptable. They’re asking whether the target deserves it. And those are completely different issues.

When “Is This OK?” Becomes “Do They Deserve It?”

At some level, most people recognize that posting someone’s personal information, contacting their employer, or coordinating harassment crosses a line. Those actions don’t suddenly become justifiable or ethical just because the person on the receiving end said something offensive. But they aren't always viewed through the same lens.

Instead, how those actions are viewed starts to hinge on the target. If the person is seen as deserving—because of what they said, what they represent, or what people assume about them—then the response starts to feel more defensible. Not necessarily good, but acceptable. Maybe even justified.

That pattern shows up in more systematic ways as well. In a series of studies conducted by Giovanno et al. (2026), participants were presented with scenarios involving organizations that held some form of authority. In some cases, those organizations were described as corrupt; in others, they weren’t. The researchers were interested in whether people would view illegal attacks against those organizations as legitimate.

What they found was fairly consistent. When participants were given information suggesting the organization was corrupt, they reported more schadenfreude—some degree of satisfaction at the idea of harm coming to that organization—and were more likely to judge illegal attacks against it as legitimate.

But the relationship wasn’t direct or automatic. The effect of perceived corruption operated in part through participants’ emotional response. In other words, it wasn’t just that people thought the organization was bad—it was that the organization’s misfortune started to feel warranted, which made the attacks themselves easier to justify.

None of that is especially surprising on its own. Feeling some degree of satisfaction when something bad happens to a disliked target doesn’t automatically flip a moral switch. But it does seem to change what starts to feel defensible.

The key is that the target has to be disliked to begin with. Without that, the emotional response doesn’t really get off the ground. But once it’s there, it does something subtle. It makes the misfortune feel earned. And once that happens, the evaluation of the response starts to change.

The question shifts. Instead of asking, “Is this kind of response acceptable?” people start asking something closer to, “Given who this is and what they did, isn’t this at least understandable?” That’s a much easier question to answer in the affirmative.

From there, reasoning tends to follow. People can point to fairness, accountability, consequences—whatever helps make the reaction feel coherent. The justification doesn’t have to be especially strong. It just has to be good enough to support the conclusion that already feels right.

This Isn’t Just About Extreme Cases

The results of the study don’t just relate to extreme cases like doxxing. The same basic pattern shows up in more ordinary situations.

Someone you don’t like gets publicly criticized. A colleague you’ve had issues with gets called out in a meeting. A public figure you disagree with says something clumsy and ends up facing consequences that seem out of proportion to what they actually did. The scale is different, but the underlying process isn’t. The reaction often depends less on the nature of what happened and more on who it happened to.

And that’s where things start to get a tiny bit messy.

Because once the target determines the judgment, consistency becomes hard to maintain. The same action can be condemned in one case and defended in another. But it’s not because the action itself changed; it’s because the person on the receiving end did.

Why It Feels Consistent—Even When It Isn’t

From the outside, that reaction looks like hypocrisy. But from the inside, it rarely feels that way.1

Different targets activate different values. What feels like fairness in one case can feel like overreach in another. What seems excessive when directed at someone you agree with can feel appropriate when directed at someone you don’t. The reasoning that follows tends to stay aligned with whichever values are most active in that moment.

That’s part of why pointing out inconsistency usually doesn’t do much. If the judgment already feels principled, being told it’s contradictory doesn’t really move the needle. It just feels like the other person isn’t seeing the situation the right way.

It also helps explain why more evidence doesn’t necessarily resolve these disagreements. Evidence doesn’t determine which values are in play. It gets interpreted through them. Two people can look at the same situation and come away with very different conclusions about what was justified—because they’re evaluating it against different standards that aren't consistently applied.

Part of what makes this difficult to catch is that it doesn’t feel like a compromise in the moment. It feels like making a reasonable distinction. Of course, this case is different. Of course, this person is different. Of course, the response makes sense here.

But that’s exactly how the shift happens. The move from criticism to justification doesn’t usually involve a clear decision point. It happens gradually, as the focus moves away from the action and toward the target. Once the target is seen as deserving, the rest tends to follow.

Which means the real issue isn’t just whether people are willing to justify harmful or even illegal behavior. It’s how often that justification is already in motion before the reasoning even begins—simply because they feel the target deserves it.

item.title: When Change Makes You Doubt Yourself
item.description:
Self-Talk

When Change Makes You Doubt Yourself

Why we turn on ourselves under pressure, and what it costs.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • When change shakes our confidence, we turn on ourselves, and self-criticism drains us faster than the change.
  • A wiser and kinder inner voice helps us think clearly, adapt, and take the next small step through change.
  • Asking for help is how we learn together through change, rather than struggling alone.

When you're struggling with workplace changes, who do you blame?

The shifting market conditions requiring another pivot? The out-of-touch executives sitting around a boardroom table? The tired team members who no longer seem to care? Or yourself?

Our research, in different countries and at different times, keeps finding that when our confidence in change wobbles, the first person we point the finger of blame at is ... ourselves.

We tie ourselves in knots of self-doubt, let our inner critic get way too loud, and become ashamed to ask for help. Then, we work harder, faster, and longer hours, hoping to figure it out. And when that doesn't work, we start avoiding the changes or complaining about them loudly to others.

“When we're navigating changes—whether we chose them or not—we often expect perfection of ourselves, but that's not reality,” explained Kristin Neff, one of the world's leading researchers on self-compassion when we interviewed her recently on a podcast. “We all bump up against our limitations, fall short of our ideals, and make mistakes. That is the human condition. It is how we learn and grow.”

“I'm the Reason This Isn't Working”

The first thing changes tend to shake is our trust in ourselves. When we're pushed outside our comfort zone, self-judgment tends to show up fast and point out: if I were better at this, it wouldn't be this hard.

“When we feel threatened, our nervous system is designed to activate our fight, flight, freeze, fawn or flop stress responses,” explained Neff. “And when we turn that fear inward, because we think we've made a mistake or we feel overwhelmed, we start fighting ourselves.”

While being self-critical may feel like we're holding ourselves accountable, researchers have found that negative self-talk shifts our brain into a state of self-punishment that leaves us stuck in a cycle of rumination and procrastination. For example, in studies following hundreds of people chasing all kinds of goals, from losing weight to lifting their performance, the more they criticized themselves, the slower their progress and the less likely they were to reach them.

Instead, dialing down our self-judgment and dialing up our self-kindness to activate our brain's caregiving and self-awareness systems makes it easier to believe we are capable and worthy. Think of your self-kind voice as a wise and supportive mentor, friend, or family member who's encouraging you to see things in a clearer and more balanced way as you figure out what's working well and where you're struggling with the changes.

Try this for yourself: When you're struggling with a change, ask: “What are my feelings telling me about this change? What would someone who believes in me and cares for me say to me right now?”

Try this for others: Share examples with others about how you talk to yourself when you're struggling through change. When you name your limitations and mistakes without the self-flagellation, it shows everyone else it's safe to be a learner, too.

“I Need More Control”

The second thing changes disrupt is our confidence to learn and adapt. As uncertainty increases, we start to grip harder, trying to control what we can: over-planning, redoing other people's work, and refusing to let go until it's right.

“When we're stressed or uncertain, we can over-identify with our thoughts and emotions and become so fused with the problem we can't think outside the box,” explained Neff.

When our perspective is lost, we can't do the one thing change requires: sense, learn, and adapt as it unfolds. Researchers have found that mindfulness, the simple act of noticing what's happening without being swept away by it, calms the stress response and helps us respond to what's in front of us rather than react on autopilot.

Try this for yourself: Mindfully create some space between yourself and the problem by naming what's happening: “I feel uncertain. This is stressful. Some of this is beyond my control.” Then ask yourself: “What is the next best small step I can own?”

Try this for others: Check in regularly as change unfolds and keep asking: What is this change teaching us about our strengths and struggles? How do we want to adapt our approach?

“I Don't Need Your Help”

The third thing changes erode is our courage to ask for help. As the struggle drags on, we convince ourselves we should be able to handle it alone, so we go quiet, hide how hard it is, and try to press on by ourselves.

“When we feel like we can't hack it the way everyone else seemingly can, we feel isolated, like there's something wrong with us,” explained Neff. “Back in the day, being cast out by the group was a threat to our survival, so needing help can still register as something to fear.”

Needing help is simply the shared experience of being wired for imperfection so we can learn, grow, and evolve. And each request, whether answered or not, builds trust with others by saying “I value what you know.” Researchers have found that when we treat our struggle as part of our common humanity, our threat response settles, and asking for help starts to feel like learning together instead of failing alone.

Try this for yourself: Acknowledge what you're finding difficult. Share why this change matters to you with someone who may be able to help. Then ask clearly and cleanly (no manipulation, passive-aggression, or need to control) for exactly what you need and when.

Try this for others: Make it easier to ask by holding “Help Huddles” where people can share what they are struggling with around the change and name one act of support that would make this easier.

When You Catch Yourself Turning Inward

So next time a change knocks you sideways, and you feel that finger of blame swing back toward yourself, notice it. The exhaustion and overwhelm you're carrying are worth listening to. It's often a sign that the way you're treating yourself has become the hardest part of the change.

item.title: The Sad Irony of Our Hybrid Empowerment
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Sad Irony of Our Hybrid Empowerment

Four steps to avoid giving more than you gain from AI.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • AI is increasingly part of how we formulate questions, interpret evidence, and decide what deserves attention.
  • Our skills erode because AI is always available and independent practice feels inefficient.
  • When the system fails, control returns to the person whose readiness has been weakened by its success.
Agency decay is not an irreversible verdict, yet. It resembles a limb kept in a cast: The capacity remains, yet strength and coordination diminish through disuse.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT, 2026

We are taking part in a global social experiment, largely without signing up. Every day, drivers request directions for routes they once knew. Writers open a chat window before facing a blank page. Hospitals, courts, and employers lean further on model-generated scores. Each choice appears minor. Together, they alter where knowledge resides, who exercises judgment, and what happens when the system fails. Tools may empower us to do more, faster at lower cost. But what are the costs?

The consequences of generative artificial intelligence (AI) go far beyond the convenience once offered by elevators or calculators. AI has entered the thought process itself. It is increasingly woven into the chain through which we formulate questions, interpret evidence, and decide what deserves attention. But AI-powered empowerment is an oxymoron. When individuals and institutions continuously transfer creation, judgment, execution, and information to a system, they gradually lose the ability to create, grasp, and master the processes that the tool was only meant to make better. Ergo, the tool is empowered at the expense of those who deploy it.

Agency decay—the luring danger of compounding comfort

Agency decay is not an irreversible verdict, yet. It resembles a limb kept in a cast: the capacity remains, yet strength and coordination diminish through disuse. Skills rarely disappear in one dramatic moment. They erode because the tool is always available, the shortcut is rewarded, and independent practice begins to feel inefficient.

The pattern predates generative AI. In “Ironies of Automation,” psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge showed already in 1983 that as automated systems become more reliable, human operators get less practice handling the situations for which they are still held responsible. When the system fails, control returns to the person whose readiness has been weakened by its success.

Memory research found a related effect. A study published in 2011 showed that when people expect information to remain available online, they remember where to retrieve it more readily than the information itself. GPS research likewise found that heavier lifetime reliance on navigation systems was associated with weaker spatial-memory performance. We did not suddenly become less intelligent; we adapted to the environment and stopped retaining what the environment promised to supply, to only remember the shortcuts to access that supply.

Early findings on generative AI deserve caution, yet they point in the same direction. A 2025 MIT Media Lab preprint reported weaker neural connectivity among participants writing essays with an AI assistant than among those working without one. Microsoft researchers surveying 319 knowledge workers found that greater confidence in generative AI was associated with less critical-thinking effort, while greater confidence in one’s own ability was associated with more. The constructive goal is hybrid intelligence: artificial assets extending natural intelligence, rather than gradually replacing its exercise.

The reverse power paradox

AI appears to give us more information. In practice, the flow can reverse. The system receives our prompts, documents, corrections, preferences, operating rules, and process histories. It accumulates context while the user may retain less of the reasoning that produced the result. The machine becomes more informed about the work as the human becomes less able to reconstruct, challenge, or perform it independently.

At the organizational level, this becomes collective agency decay. Companies are not only buying software; many are embedding external AI systems into research, customer service, coding, recruitment, logistics, and strategic analysis. They transfer proprietary data and operational knowledge into tools that increasingly mediate how work is done. Over time, part of the organization’s practical intelligence migrates beyond its boundary.

The dependency is technical, commercial, and cognitive. Data may be difficult to move. Processes are redesigned around a provider’s models and interfaces. Staff stop practicing the underlying work. Switching supplier then means more than replacing a license: It can require extracting data, rebuilding workflows, retraining people, and recovering capabilities that have atrophied. Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) work on data portability links poor interoperability to higher switching costs and lock-in, while the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) generative-AI risk profile explicitly advises organizations to identify overreliance on third-party data and systems, maintain fallbacks, and scrutinize vendor arrangements.

When oversight becomes theatre

“Human oversight” is often presented as the safeguard. Yet there is a big “but”—oversight is only meaningful when the overseer understands the task, the system’s limits, and the evidence needed to contest its output. A person who cannot reproduce the reasoning, recognize a plausible error, or act without the tool is not supervising it. They are authorizing it.

This takes the aforementioned irony of sophisticated automation to an institutional scale. As systems grow more capable, organizations may retain a human approval step while removing the knowledge, time, and authority that make approval substantive. The European Union AI Act reflects the underlying requirement by linking oversight to competent, trained, and authorized human beings. A signature at the end of an opaque process cannot substitute for informed judgment. Ultimately, the human decision-maker must remain accountable.

AI-mediated peer review offers a vivid example. Automating parts of evaluation may relieve an overloaded academic system. Yet handing over the judgment that determines which ideas a field rewards also shifts intellectual steering toward patterns favored by the model... The same distinction applies in business: Delegating a first draft is different from delegating the decision about what should be built at all, whom it should affect, and which risks are acceptable.

The following is a simple four-step process to be and remain proactive players in a hybrid landscape:

The A-Frame takeaway

Awareness: Notice which abilities, data, and decisions are moving from yourself, your team, and your institution into AI systems.

Appreciation: Value AI’s speed and reach, alongside human capacity—starting with your own—to critically question, contextualize, and imagine from scratch.

Acceptance: Friction is part of competence. Most relevant tasks must be learned and practiced before they can be delegated safely.

Accountability: Before using AI, ask not only, “Can it do this?” Ask: “Could we understand, defend, and continue this work without it—and why do we need AI in this context at all?”

We can still do something to preserve our place in the hybrid driver’s seat. But for how much longer?

item.title: Finding Your Way to Stronger Connections
item.description:
Relationships

Finding Your Way to Stronger Connections

Navigating contradictory advice for more satisfying relationships.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Relationship advice often seems contradictory because different goals require different strategies.
  • Applying the same relationship strategy across the board can lead to conflict.
  • The Relationship Compass helps you choose actions that align with your interpersonal goals.

If you've ever searched for relationship advice online, you've probably noticed that much of it is contradictory.

One expert tells you to be more vulnerable. Another reminds you to protect your boundaries. Some encourage forgiveness after conflict, while others warn against tolerating behavior that hurts you. You're told to ask for what you need but also not to expect anyone to meet your needs.

Which of these recommendations are correct? The frustrating answer is it depends.

Most of the common relationship advice is perfectly sound—in certain contexts. For example, one of my clients came to a session one day and proudly announced that she was "working on her boundaries." She excitedly told me how she'd said no when a friend was pressuring her to join an expensive girls' trip she couldn't really afford. Great boundary.

Then she told me she'd done the same thing when the man she'd recently started dating texted that afternoon to see if she wanted to grab dinner, explaining, "I can't reward last-minute plans." I knew she really liked this guy and wanted to get closer, so I asked her, “Do you actually mind that he texted the same day, or did you say no because you've decided that's what healthy people do?"

That's when I realized we often treat relationship advice as though it's universally applicable. In reality, the best strategy depends on the direction you're trying to go in any given relationship.

The Four Directions

This realization became the idea behind the “The Relationship Compass,” a framework my colleagues and I developed as part of a new treatment for borderline personality disorder (BPD). Although it was designed for people who struggle with intense emotions and unstable relationships, I've found it to be helpful for almost anyone.

Rather than telling you exactly what to do, the Relationship Compass helps you identify the direction you want a relationship to move before deciding how to act. It has four primary directions, each representing a different interpersonal goal:

  1. Need something. Sometimes the healthiest direction is asking for something you need, whether that's practical help or more emotional support.

  2. Set a limit. Sometimes the relationship can only remain healthy if you establish a boundary. A limit isn't about punishing someone else or closing yourself off. It's about protecting your own well-being and living in accordance with your values.

  3. Want the relationship. At other times, the relationship itself is the priority. You may want to strengthen a friendship, deepen intimacy with a partner, reconnect with a family member, or build trust with someone new. This direction asks, "What behaviors are likely to move us closer?"

  4. End the relationship. Finally, there are situations in which the healthiest path is creating permanent distance. It may be the action most consistent with your safety, well-being, or long-term values.

article continues after advertisement

The Relationship Compass isn't limited to the four cardinal directions. Just as a real compass points northeast or southwest, relationships often require us to move in more than one direction at once. You might both want the relationship and need to set a limit, for instance.

Once you've identified the direction, choosing your next step becomes much easier.

When You Need Something

One of the most common mistakes people make is assuming that if someone loves them, they should automatically know what they need. When that doesn't happen, it's easy to become resentful or to communicate indirectly through hints, sarcasm, or even withdrawing. Others overcorrect in the opposite direction, demanding what they need so intensely that the conversation becomes about the delivery rather than the request itself. Both strategies usually leave people feeling misunderstood.

A more effective approach is to ask assertively. A conversation to ask for what you need should start with setting the stage by describing the situation objectively, followed by sharing the emotion you’re experiencing. Then, you make a direct request, explaining how it will help you in the current situation. Asking clearly doesn't guarantee you'll get what you want, but it gives the other person the best opportunity to respond.

When You Need to Set a Limit

Boundary advice is everywhere these days, but it's often presented as though saying "no" is always the healthiest response. In reality, healthy boundaries are balanced. Saying yes to everything can leave you exhausted and resentful, while saying no to everything makes it difficult to build relationships based on trust and mutual support.

Rather than simply refusing a request, explain what's making the situation difficult for you, acknowledge the other person's perspective, and offer an alternative when appropriate. A well-set limit protects both your well-being and the relationship itself.

When You Want the Relationship

If your goal is building connections, many of the behaviors that feel safest can actually move you in the opposite direction from what you want. People who fear rejection often stay quiet or avoid sharing personal information so they don’t get hurt. These behaviors reduce anxiety in the short term, but they also make genuine closeness harder to achieve.

article continues after advertisement

Building relationships usually requires tolerating some uncertainty. Showing curiosity by asking questions, expressing appreciation, making eye contact, sharing your thoughts and feelings, and creating opportunities to spend time together all communicate interest in ways that strengthen connection over time. These actions may feel vulnerable, but vulnerability is often the price for intimacy.

When It's Time to End the Relationship

Boilerplate advice often tells us to leave at the first sign of conflict, or, conversely, to fight for every relationship no matter the cost. Neither extreme is particularly helpful. Some relationships deserve repair, while others repeatedly undermine your safety, dignity, or values.

When you're considering ending a relationship, try to make the decision from a place of reflection rather than emotional urgency. One exercise we use in BPD Compass is listing the pros and cons of both staying and leaving. Slowing down in this way helps ensure that your decision reflects your long-term values instead of how you’re feeling in the moment.

The Best Relationship Advice Depends on Where You're Going

The Relationship Compass has changed the way I think about interpersonal problems because it reminds me that there isn't one universally "correct" relationship skill. The same behavior—being vulnerable, setting a boundary, asking for support, or walking away—can be exactly what’s needed in one situation, but backfire in another.

Before deciding what to say or do, pause and ask yourself a simpler question: Where do I want this relationship to go? Once your destination is clear, the next step often becomes much easier to identify.

item.title: The Psychedelic Window Always Closes
item.description:
Psychedelics

The Psychedelic Window Always Closes

You think the psychedelic experience is the breakthrough. It’s only the beginning.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • A psychedelic experience opens a window of mental flexibility. When it closes, the insight rarely survives.
  • Research suggests the real change isn't the experience but what gets encoded while the brain is flexible.
  • Drawing a durable picture of what you experienced, before the window shuts, is what makes it durable.

Danny emerged from a guided psilocybin session lit up in a way he’d never been in years of therapy. He'd spent his whole life believing that if he ever stopped performing, he'd disappear, that his worth was his output. For five hours, that belief simply let go of him. He saw his kids' faces. He understood, in his body, that he was already enough. He wept. He called it the most important day of his life.

He thought he’d figured out the answer to his life’s problems, but I knew better… I’d seen this over a hundred times before. If he didn't do the work, he'd be back to where he started within a few weeks.

(Danny is a composite drawn from numerous people I've worked with.)

If you've done psychedelic work or sat with someone who has, you know this story. The mountaintop, and then the slow, baffling slide back down. And here's the part almost everyone misses: That slide is not a failure of willpower, or proof the experience was fake. It's biology doing exactly what biology does.

We've all felt a version of it. The retreat that changed everything, but didn't stick. The podcast insight is so clear you couldn't imagine forgetting, but somehow forgot by Friday.

The window is real. So is the wall it's cut into.

Here's a metaphor I use with every client who does this work.

Most of your life, you've been living in a room. The walls are the beliefs you built long ago to keep yourself safe—I have to earn love; I can't be seen struggling; if I stop, I'm nothing. You didn't choose the room. You inherited it, or built it as a kid with the materials you had, and then you forgot it was built at all. You just called it "reality."

A psychedelic experience opens a window in that room.

Suddenly, there's light from a direction you've never seen. You look out, and there's a whole world your walls had been blocking. You can see the ocean, palm trees blowing in the wind. A whole set of worldviews and feelings you’ve never known before. It's genuinely new information, and it's really yours.

You feel incredible. You’re sure you’ve seen the light.

But then the window closes. It always does. It's supposed to. And when it closes, if all you did was stand there admiring the view, you're right back in the same room, armed with a bittersweet memory of what you’d seen through that window.

The work, the entire work, is about what you do while the window is open. If you want it to last, you have to draw a picture of what you see out there, so that when the wall goes opaque again, you're not left with a fading feeling. You're left with a representation you can hold, study, and build from.

What the window actually is

This isn't mysticism. It maps onto some of the most interesting neuroscience of the last decade.

Your brain runs on prediction. High-level beliefs sit at the top and filter everything below them. Most of what you "perceive" is really your own expectations confirming themselves. Neuroscientists Robin Carhart-Harris and Karl Friston proposed that psychedelics work by relaxing the grip of those top-down beliefs. Their model, REBUS (RElaxed Beliefs Under pSychedelics), suggests psychedelics briefly let bottom-up experience flood through less filtered. That's the window opening: the walls, for a few hours, stop filtering your view.

And the glass is more than a metaphor. In animals, a single dose of psilocybin produced rapid, lasting growth of new connections between neurons in the frontal cortex within 24 hours, and it was still present a month later. Other research found that several psychedelics reopen a "critical period," a state of heightened learning the brain normally reserves for childhood, and that the window stays open roughly as long as the experience itself lasts.

Think about what that means. The experience doesn't hand you a new self. It hands you a window of unusual flexibility. A few hours when the old wiring is genuinely revisable. What gets built in that window is up to you.

Why insight alone evaporates

Why do clients slide back? Because they treat the insight as the finish line. They see the view and assume seeing is enough.

But a brain that has briefly relaxed its old beliefs will, without new input, revert back. Those old beliefs are well-worn, efficient, and familiar. Seeing outside the window doesn't rewrite the room. Only encoding something new while the window is open does.

Here's the most hopeful finding of all, and notice it involves no drug at all. When old memories, including old fears, are reactivated, a brief window opens in which the memory is chemically "unlocked." If we feed in new, non-threatening information, the fearful memory can be replaced. When done right, the fear doesn’t return, not the next day and not a year later. That window is called reconsolidation.

That is the scientific heart of the metaphor. Drawing the picture is the edit. When you actively externalize what you saw—in words, in writing, in a new habit—you're not just journaling a nice memory. You're wiring in new information while it's still soft.

You're making a picture of what you saw through the window.

What to do while the window is open

This is what I take clients through and what I do myself. It's the picture that makes the experience pay off:

  1. Name the room before you go looking for the window. Before any experience, get specific about the beliefs you battle with. You can't redraw a wall you can't see. Write them down in a few sentences.
  2. Draw the picture in the moment, then again within 48 hours. During and right after, capture what you saw in concrete language. Not "I felt love," but "I know I am enough, even when I produce nothing [write the evidence, as you feel it in your mind and body]." Return to it deliberately within two days, while the wiring is still pliable. Say it out loud. Edit your notes, focusing on the new belief. The goal isn't to remember the trip. It's to install the correction.
  3. Give the picture a body. Insight that stays in your head fades with the window. Insight that becomes a behavior gets encoded by repetition. Commit to one different choice you make this week that only makes sense if the new belief is true. That’s the practice that outlasts any single window. For Danny, it was writing down what he’s grateful for as he closed his laptop for the evening. Small. Concrete. A window, re-drawn.

Remember this

The window is a gift, but it's on loan. It opens, it shows you a world your walls were hiding, and then it closes, every time, by design. What you keep isn't the view. It's the picture you drew while you could still see.

So the next time the glass goes clear, don't just stand there. Pick up the pen or a crayon. Draw fast, draw honestly, and draw something you can live inside after the light is gone.

What would you draw if the window opened tomorrow?

For more on the hidden drivers behind the patterns we can't seem to outrun, see my book Unhooked.

item.title: How Trauma-Related Schemas Shape Your Life
item.description:
Trauma

How Trauma-Related Schemas Shape Your Life

Childhood trauma creates painful schemas in your brain, but they can be healed.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Childhood trauma creates painful mental schemas, which shape your thoughts, feelings, and behaviour.
  • These schemas can be healed with trauma-informed approaches like schema therapy.
  • As schemas loosen their grip, your thoughts become more helpful and you feel calmer, happier, and stronger.
Source: Renaud Confavreux/Unsplash

This is the first post in a series.

We now know that childhood trauma is far more widespread than mental health professionals previously understood. And traumatic experiences are on a spectrum, from milder to more severe. While the focus had been on profoundly traumatic experiences such as physical or sexual abuse, many experts now argue that apparently milder experiences, such as being bullied or growing up in a high-conflict home, can also be traumatic for kids. These traumatic experiences are mediated by a child’s temperament and their core emotional needs.

If these developmental needs were not met for you on a consistent basis, you might have developed one or more painful mental schemas.1 In this first of two posts, we will examine two of these schemas. It is a good idea to read the description of each schema and then make some notes about whether it resonates with you or not. If you would like to check which of the schemas you have, take the Young Schema Questionnaire (YSQ), which is available on Dr. Young’s website.2

Abandonment/Instability

This schema often develops when you’re a small child. You may have lost a caregiver when you were little—perhaps you were adopted and given up by your birth parents. Or one of your parents might have died, which would have been extremely painful and potentially life-changing. But often, people with this schema didn’t physically lose anyone, so it’s helpful to look at part two of the schema: Instability. This means instability of attachment; estimates suggest that around 50 percent of the population has an insecure attachment style.

Perhaps your mother had postnatal depression, so she struggled to connect with you (through no fault of her own). For a tiny baby, this can feel agonizing because every time your mum was shut down and withdrawn, averting her gaze or just being unresponsive, you would have felt abandoned. To a small baby, who is not capable of thought or understanding and just feels intense bodily sensations and overwhelming emotions, this feeling of abandonment would have been unbearable, so the schema would start to take hold.

As an adult, this schema can be especially tricky in your relationships because it can make you deeply insecure. You may be plagued by jealousy, obsessively checking your partner’s phone for signs they are cheating. You could also go the other way, refusing to commit for fear of being left, so engaging in a string of safe-but-meaningless flings.

Let’s examine this schema through Shazia’s story. Her family moved to the UK from Pakistan before she was born. Shazia remembers an idyllic childhood in her large, loving family until her beloved mother died suddenly when she was eight. "It was like my world turned upside-down. I was so happy as a child and my mum was everything to me," she recalled with a shaky voice. She was raised by her grandmother, who could not fill the void left by her mother’s passing. "I used to cry myself to sleep every night," she said. "I missed Mum so much, it was agony."

Despite the family’s best efforts, she never got over the loss of her mother, which led to periods of deep, grief-stricken depression in adolescence. At the same time, Shazia started dating girls, which was a different kind of turmoil. "Dad was very traditional and strict," she told me. "He would never have accepted me as gay—I would have been thrown out. And being with someone was horrible. When I liked a girl I got crazy-jealous and picked fights all the time. I was a nightmare."

Shazia was so insecure and volatile that her girlfriends got fed up and left, strengthening her Abandonment schema and her belief that everyone would leave in the end. When she came for therapy, we first had to link her romantic behaviour to the tragic loss of her mother, then gradually heal her Abandonment schema. We also helped her realize that love and trust with a partner were possible, which eventually allowed her to start dating again. After a few false starts, much to her surprise and delight, Shazia found a secure, stable relationship for the first time in her life.

Mistrust/Abuse

If you experienced any kind of abuse as a child—physical, sexual, or emotional—you are likely to have this schema. It forms through repeated experiences of being hurt, betrayed, manipulated, or let down. Like the previous schema, this one might start early and so be particularly intense. Both schemas can be preverbal, developing before your infant brain developed the power of language, so when they get triggered now, you may feel intense emotions like fear or rage, without any thoughts to explain them, making these feelings confusing and scary. You might also experience dissociation, feeling spaced out or detached.

This schema will be triggered in relationships, which might feel deeply unsafe. You may be on your guard, feel you cannot be vulnerable, and think that other people are unpredictable or even dangerous. You may expect people to hurt, betray, or use you. And when someone does something nice, you may assume there is an ulterior motive and expect people to take advantage of you. In my consulting room, I see many clients with this schema and explain to them that the key is to move from universal mistrust to selective mistrust. Instead of thinking, "People are out to get me, I can’t trust anyone," it’s much more helpful (and accurate) to think, "Some people are not to be trusted, that’s true—people do lie. But many people are kind and decent, so I will judge people on their behaviour, not assume they are guilty until proven innocent."

These clients can also be mistrustful of me and therapists/authority figures in general. So I help them learn to trust me, little by little, then expand that trust to people they know. If this is true of you, learning to trust those people who behave in consistently trustworthy ways will help you develop more satisfying, fulfilling relationships. Otherwise, life might feel bereft of love, richness, and meaning because for social mammals like humans, connected, mutually supportive relationships are the cornerstone of a happy life.

This post has been adapted from my new book, Heal Your Trauma: How to Overcome a Painful Childhood to Become Happy and Whole Again.
